pages.x: After bad harvests and hard times, Paris rose in February 1848, and King Louis Philippe slipped away to England in disguise. France became a republic again. The news spread fast, and within weeks crowds were building barricades in Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Munich and Budapest.

Weeks before, two young Germans, Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, had published a pamphlet in London for a small workers' league. The Communist Manifesto began by saying that a spectre was haunting Europe, the spectre of communism, and ended by calling on the workers of all countries to unite. Few read it then; in the next century it shaped the lives of millions.

In Vienna students and workers rose in March. Prince Metternich, who had kept the old order in Europe since Napoleon's fall, resigned and fled to England. The emperor promised a constitution, and that autumn the empire's peasants were freed from the unpaid work they owed their lords: one change of 1848 that lasted.

In May hundreds of elected men met in St Paul's Church in Frankfurt to make one Germany out of its 39 states. They argued for nearly a year about its rights and its borders. When they finally offered the crown of all Germany to the king of Prussia, he turned it down, calling it in private a crown from the gutter.

Hungary went furthest. Led by Lajos Kossuth, a lawyer and fiery speaker, it won its own government, went to war with Austria, and in April 1849 declared itself independent. The young emperor Franz Joseph asked the tsar for help, and some 200,000 Russian soldiers marched in. In August the Hungarians surrendered.

The rebels were split: middle-class liberals wanted constitutions, workers wanted bread and jobs, and nationalists wanted countries of their own, often on the same land. One by one the old rulers' armies took back control. In France voters made Napoleon's nephew president, and in 1852 he made himself emperor.

Thousands of beaten revolutionaries fled abroad. Many Germans settled in the United States, where these Forty-Eighters started newspapers, spoke out against slavery and fought for the Union in the Civil War. Kossuth toured America to cheering crowds.

Almost every revolution of 1848 failed, but much of what the rebels wanted came later. Serfdom never came back in Austria, Prussia and Piedmont kept parliaments, and within a generation Italy and Germany were united, though by kings and generals rather than by the people.
